title: Automated Testing Strategy
requirement: Experience with automated testing: unit, integration, and end-to-end tests across the stack.

questions.question: What makes a good unit test, and what do the arrange-act-assert stages enforce?
questions.answer: A good unit test is fast, deterministic and fails for one readable reason. I use arrange, act, assert and test behavior, not implementation, so it survives refactors. If I need heavy mocking to run a test, that's design feedback about too many dependencies.
questions.keyTakeaway: Fast, deterministic, behavior-focused tests with one reason to fail; mocking pain is design feedback.

questions.question: What should you test in a React component, and why is querying implementation details an anti-pattern?
questions.answer: I test what the user experiences: rendered content, roles, labels and interactions, using queries like getByRole that mirror how users find things. Querying by class name or internal state couples the test to structure, so harmless refactors break it. After an invalid submit I assert the error message, not a state variable.
questions.keyTakeaway: Test rendered behavior through user-facing queries; implementation-coupled assertions break on refactors, not bugs.

questions.question: What is the difference between a mock, a stub, a fake, and a spy?
questions.answer: A stub returns canned answers, a mock also asserts interactions, and a fake is a lightweight working version like an in-memory repository. I stub and fake inputs, and mock only at side-effect boundaries like charging a card. I never mock what I don't own, so I wrap vendor SDKs in my own interface.
questions.keyTakeaway: Stub inputs, mock only side-effect contracts, prefer fakes for behavior, never mock what you don't own.

questions.question: Where do you draw the line between unit and integration tests, and how do you make integration tests fast enough to run on every push?
questions.answer: Unit tests check logic with doubles at the edges. Integration tests check real pieces wired together, which is where most production bugs live: bad SQL, wrong transactions, serialization. I keep them fast with an ephemeral database started once per suite and a fresh schema per test, and I use factories, not shared seed data.
questions.keyTakeaway: Integration-test the real wiring with per-test isolated databases; contract-check repositories once instead of everywhere.

questions.question: How do you build an end-to-end suite that catches real regressions without becoming flaky and slow?
questions.answer: I keep E2E small, only the journeys that define the product like signup, login and checkout. Everything else is cheaper at the integration layer. I use Playwright with auto-waiting, role-based selectors and no sleeps. Each test creates its own user through the API, so they run in parallel and in any order.
questions.keyTakeaway: Few critical journeys, role-based auto-waiting selectors, isolated per-test state, zero tolerated flake.

questions.question: What causes flaky tests, and how do you systematically eliminate them?
questions.answer: The causes are shared mutable state, fixed sleeps, slow external dependencies and order dependence. I fix them with hygiene, not retries: reset state in setup, unique data per test, randomized order, injected clocks. Retries hide the problem and train the team to ignore red. A flaky test gets an owner and is quarantined that day.
questions.keyTakeaway: Flake is shared state, timing, or hidden order dependence; quarantine and fix it, never train red to be normal.

questions.question: Is code coverage a useful metric? How do you use it without gaming it?
questions.answer: Coverage is a useful negative signal and a weak positive one. Low coverage means the change is unverified, but high coverage only proves the code ran. So I ratchet on diff coverage with no global target, and use mutation testing to see whether tests actually fail when the code changes.
questions.keyTakeaway: Ratchet diff coverage, let mutation testing catch empty tests, and never let the metric become the goal.

questions.question: How would you build the test strategy for a payments feature where bugs cost real money?
questions.answer: I rank by blast radius, so money gets the deepest layers. Unit tests cover amount math, rounding, partial refunds and state transitions. Integration tests use Stripe test mode and replay webhooks against real handlers, including duplicate and out-of-order ones, since that's where payments break. A couple of E2E tests cover checkout, and I alert on anomalous refund rates.
questions.keyTakeaway: Depth where money moves: deterministic unit math, test-mode integration with webhooks, reconciliation drift tests, production rate alarms.

questions.question: You inherit a legacy module with zero tests that the business depends on: how do you make it safe to change?
questions.answer: I characterize before I refactor. I write tests that pin what the code does today, oddities included, so any accidental change fails loudly. Then I break dependency cycles just enough to instantiate it. Mechanical refactors are verified by that suite, and behavior changes get their tests updated first. Each diff is structure or semantics, never both.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pin current behavior with characterization tests, create seams, then separate structural refactors from behavior changes.

diagram.title: Making legacy code safe to change

questions.question: How do contract tests keep independent services from breaking each other?
questions.answer: Consumer tests publish a pact file, and the provider verifies it against its real implementation in CI. So a field the consumer uses can't be renamed without a red provider build. That replaces shared integration environments and mocks that drift. A broker stores the pacts and can-i-deploy gates the release.
questions.keyTakeaway: Consumer-driven pacts verified in provider CI turn 'it broke integration' into a red build before deploy.

questions.question: How do you keep test data maintainable when hundreds of tests need slightly different versions of the same domain objects?
questions.answer: I use builders. A builder makes a valid domain object with sensible defaults, and each test overrides only the fields it cares about. An active user with an expired card is one fluent line, not a forty-field literal. I never share mutable instances between tests.
questions.keyTakeaway: Builders with valid defaults age well; override only what the behavior cares about and never share mutable fixtures.

questions.question: When is snapshot testing a good idea, and how do you stop snapshots from becoming noise nobody reviews?
questions.answer: Snapshots fit small, stable output like generated SQL. They rot on large component trees: the first is committed unread, someone presses update, and the test verifies nothing. So I read snapshot diffs like code review and keep them short. If I only care about part of a render, I write a specific assertion.
questions.keyTakeaway: Snapshots work only when small and reviewed like code; a blindly updated diff verifies nothing.

questions.question: How would you introduce visual regression testing without drowning the team in false positives?
questions.answer: I screenshot only pages and components with real layout or brand risk, at fixed viewports, and run them in CI since laptop font rendering causes noise. I freeze animations and dates and seed data, then diff against committed baselines. The diff image goes in the PR, and a red test is a review request.
questions.keyTakeaway: Deterministic rendering plus CI-diffed baselines with human review turns screenshots into a real signal.

questions.question: How do you test logic that depends on the current time, like expiring tokens or debounced saves?
questions.answer: Time is the classic hidden dependency. Production code never calls Date.now inline. It asks an injected clock, or I use fake timers like vitest's useFakeTimers. Tests set a fixed instant and advance it, so I can prove a token expired in milliseconds. I also pin the time zone, since bugs hide at DST boundaries.
questions.keyTakeaway: Inject the clock or use fake timers, set a fixed time, advance it explicitly, and pin the time zone.

questions.question: What do testcontainers give you that mocking the database or sharing a dev instance cannot?
questions.answer: Testcontainers starts the real dependency from the test, like an actual Postgres in Docker. In-memory fakes lie, since H2 accepts SQL that Postgres rejects, and a shared dev database gets polluted. One container per suite, with schema or rollback isolation per test.
questions.keyTakeaway: Run the real engine in a container per suite with per-test isolation; in-memory fakes lie and shared databases pollute.

questions.question: What does it actually take to make a test suite safe to run fully in parallel?
questions.answer: Parallelism usually fails in four places: data, files, ports and globals. I use unique data per test, like UUID-based emails, remove hidden singletons and mutated environment variables, and randomize order in CI to surface coupling. For databases I pick one strategy: rollback per test, schema per test, or a container per worker.
questions.keyTakeaway: Parallel speed requires unique data, isolated files and ports, no shared globals, and one database isolation strategy.

questions.question: How do you mock network calls in frontend tests so they catch real wiring problems without coupling to implementation?
questions.answer: I mock at the network layer, not the module layer. MSW intercepts real HTTP, so the component runs its actual data-fetching client, where a module mock can hide that the request never fires. I set handlers once and override one only to stage a scenario like an error. I assert on what rendered, not that a request fired.
questions.keyTakeaway: Mock the network with MSW so real clients run; stage scenarios per test and assert on rendered outcomes.

questions.question: How do you split smoke tests from the full regression suite across the deployment pipeline?
questions.answer: Smoke tests answer one question after each deploy: is it alive and does the core path work? That's five to fifteen fast checks, like login works and health endpoints are green, and promotion is gated on them. Full regression runs earlier: unit and integration on every PR, E2E on merges or nightly. If smoke fails in production, I roll back.
questions.keyTakeaway: Smoke checks core aliveness after every deploy and gates promotion; full regression runs pre-merge and nightly.

questions.question: A test passes on your machine but fails only in CI: how do you track it down?
questions.answer: I assume CI is showing a real environment difference. I diff runtime versions, environment variables, locale and time zone, then consider what CI adds, like parallel runs exposing order coupling. I reproduce it by running the same commands in the CI image locally. I never add a retry, because it turns a diagnosable bug into a permanent one.
questions.keyTakeaway: Reproduce the CI environment faithfully and hunt order coupling; never convert a diagnosable failure into a retry.

questions.question: Where does property-based testing earn its place, and how does it complement example-based tests?
questions.answer: Property-based testing replaces hand-picked examples with generators plus an invariant that must hold for any input, like encode then decode returns the original. Libraries like fast-check generate hundreds of cases and hit forgotten corners like unicode and empty lists. A failure shrinks to a minimal counterexample, and I pin the seed as a regression.
questions.keyTakeaway: Generators plus invariants find forgotten edge cases and shrink failures to minimal counterexamples; pin seeds as regressions.

questions.question: How do you make CI run only the tests a change could affect, and where does that approach break down?
questions.answer: Nx, Turborepo and Bazel maintain a dependency graph, so I compute the affected set, changed files plus downstream targets, and run only that on the PR. A forty-minute suite becomes ninety seconds for a leaf change. But static graphs miss dynamic edges like runtime-assembled SQL, so merges to main and a nightly job run everything.
questions.keyTakeaway: Run the affected set on pull requests but keep full-suite runs on main and nightly, since static graphs miss dynamic edges.

questions.question: How much accessibility testing can you realistically automate, and where does automation fall short?
questions.answer: I automate the mechanical layer everywhere. axe-core in component tests catches things like contrast failures and unlabeled inputs, roughly the mechanical third of WCAG. I fail builds on new violations and baseline the old backlog like a coverage ratchet. Automation can't judge focus after a modal closes or alt text quality, so I schedule manual screen reader passes.
questions.keyTakeaway: Automate axe scans at every layer with a violations ratchet, and budget manual screen-reader passes for experience judgment.

questions.question: How would you add basic load testing to a backend service that has never had any?
questions.answer: I start from objectives, not tools. We agree what fine means, say p95 under 300 milliseconds at twice today's peak, then I encode that as pass-fail thresholds in a k6 script modeling real traffic and run it on staging with production-like data. I also watch CPU, connection pools and locks, since k6 shows slowness, not which tier bent first.
questions.keyTakeaway: Encode SLO thresholds in load scripts, mirror real traffic against production-like data, and watch server metrics for the bending tier.

code.snippet:
# nightly smoke-scale load check with pass-fail thresholds
k6 run --vus 20 --duration 60s scripts/load/smoke.js

# full ramp to find the ceiling before a major release
k6 run scripts/load/ramp.js --out json=results.json

questions.question: Can writing tests damage a design, and how do you test in a way that improves the code instead?
questions.answer: Tests damage design when the tail wags the dog: methods made public only for tests, test flags in production logic, classes split just to be mockable. Good testing injects dependencies at real boundaries like the database and clock, and asserts through public behavior. A painful test is feedback, so I fix the design, not the test.
questions.keyTakeaway: Never contort production code for testability; inject dependencies at real boundaries and assert through public behavior.

diagram.title: Tests that harm versus help design

questions.question: What do you look for when reviewing another engineer's tests in a pull request?
questions.answer: I read the tests before the implementation, since they show what the author thinks the behavior is. Would each test fail if that behavior broke? Is it deterministic, with no sleeps or real clocks? Does it test public behavior, not internals? Are the sad paths covered? I send back tests with weak assertions, since they run code without verifying it.
questions.keyTakeaway: A reviewed test must fail when the behavior breaks, stay deterministic and isolated, and cover error paths, not only happy paths.

questions.question: How do you test background jobs and async workflows whose results arrive after the request has returned?
questions.answer: I split it. The job handler is a function from message to outcome, so I unit-test its logic. Then I integration-test the machinery with a real broker in a testcontainer. The same message twice proves idempotency, and a poison message must retry with backoff and reach the dead-letter queue, not loop forever. I never assert on queue internals.
questions.keyTakeaway: Unit-test handler logic, integration-test delivery with idempotency, retries, and dead-lettering, and assert async outcomes with eventually polling.

questions.question: How do you decide what not to test, and when is deleting a test the right call?
questions.answer: I test where failure costs money, trust or a debugging afternoon, and skip trivial getters, third-party internals and generated code. A test's value is the chance it catches a real bug times its cost, minus what it costs in flakes and churn. I delete tests that break on harmless refactors, check behavior that no longer exists, or sit in quarantine with no owner.
questions.keyTakeaway: Every test must earn its lifetime maintenance cost; delete implementation-coupled, duplicated, or ownerless flaky tests without guilt.

diagram.title: Keep or delete a test
diagram.condition: Does it catch real bugs worth more than its upkeep?

questions.question: How do you prove that resilience code like retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers actually works?
questions.answer: Resilience code is invisible on the happy path, so I inject failure at the boundary. Fail three times then succeed, and assert a retry with backoff. Hang forever, and assert the client times out and degrades. Exceed the threshold, and assert the circuit opens, half-opens and recovers. I retry only idempotent operations.
questions.keyTakeaway: Inject failures against fakes to prove retries, timeouts, and breaker states, including idempotency and genuine cancellation.
